samples.hyp: Estimate the number of SARS-CoV-2 screening tests required for potential outbreak control in Lusaka Province, Zambia, considering the proportion of asymptomatic individuals.
Elementary mathematical analysis

The novel coronavirus (COVID-19), caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2), in Africa has a higher proportion of asymptomatic (or mildly symptomatic) individuals, believed to be contributing to the spread of the disease.
The exact number and prevalence of asymptomatic cases were not determined.
The study however showed that managing them is crucial for controlling the spread of SARS-CoV-2.

We developed a simple, readily-deployable susceptible-exposed-infectious-recovered (SEIR) mathematical model to assess the impact of isolating SARS-CoV-2 infected but asymptomatic individuals via targeted testing to control outbreaks in Lusaka Province, Zambia.
Here, we modeled two scenarios; (1) asymptomatic individuals comprising 70% of all COVID-19 infections and (2) asymptomatic individuals comprising 50% of the population.

Initially, the model was calibrated under two assumptions: first, that asymptomatic individuals have the same infectiousness as symptomatic individuals; and second, and more plausibly, that asymptomatic individuals have half the infectiousness of symptomatic individuals.

For a model that captures 70% of asymptomatic individuals, a daily screening test coverage of ≥7911 tests/100,000 population is sufficient to control the outbreak if asymptomatic individuals are half as infectious, while if infectivity is equal, a test coverage of ≥10028 tests/100,000 population will be required.

For 50% of asymptomatic individuals, a low screening test frequency of ≥ 4540 tests/100,000 population is sufficient to control outbreaks at all prevalence levels for asymptomatic individuals relative to symptomatic individuals.
Discussion and Conclusion

Our model predicts that targeted testing for COVID-19 infection, including asymptomatic individuals, using rapid diagnostic tests could be a viable measure for controlling the spread of SARS-CoV-2 in Lusaka, Zambia, but it would be costly.
Mass testing in major cities like Lusaka may limit the spread of COVID-19, but is it worthwhile?
In 2020, computer models predicted that the spread of COVID-19 in major cities could be controlled through widespread testing and the isolation of all infected individuals.
However, researchers say this method may be expensive and ineffective.
At the beginning of the pandemic outbreak, a significant proportion of individuals infected with COVID-19 were asymptomatic yet still transmitted the disease to others.
Some studies suggest that 50% to 80% of people with COVID-19 are asymptomatic and may be responsible for 40% to 70% of new infections.
Researchers wanted to know whether identifying and isolating asymptomatic individuals would help control the spread of COVID-19.
They also wanted to know whether the blanket testing approach, which means testing many people repeatedly, is effectively identifying asymptomatic individuals.
Researchers created a computer model that predicts how vulnerable people are to infection and isolation.
They focused on data from Zambia's Lusaka Province, a transportation hub and international airport bordering two countries.

Because COVID-19 symptoms appeared to vary geographically, they considered four scenarios, where either 50% or 70% of COVID-19 cases were asymptomatic, and these asymptomatic individuals were either equally or half as infectious as symptomatic individuals.
The researchers' model found that it is possible to control the spread of COVID-19 through widespread testing and isolation of all infected individuals, including those without symptoms.
They said that to reduce the peak number of infected individuals by 90% in all scenarios, 10% of the Lusaka population would need to be tested daily.
They also found that to keep the number of new COVID-19 infections constant, 22% of the population would need to be tested daily.
Despite Zambia implementing numerous COVID-19 restriction measures, infections are still rising.
Proper mask-wearing reduced COVID-19 cases by 90% in a small Italian town.
However, no previous research has shown that it would be effective in a major city elsewhere.

Note that the researchers did not actually conduct a lockdown experiment in this study; instead, they created a model that simulates how a lockdown would work to limit the spread of COVID-19 in major cities.
However, they cautioned that it would be very expensive.
They also said it could be more effective when combined with other measures, such as lockdowns, contact tracing, and vaccination.
Zambian researchers also emphasized that asymptomatic COVID-19 cases were more prevalent in Africa at that time.
High genetic diversity in African populations due to genetic and environmental factors.
African populations are underrepresented in genomic studies but exhibit high genetic diversity and experience diverse environmental exposures globally.

Because genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have not yet been conducted in the ancestral populations relevant to African genetic diversity, we calculated polygenic risk scores (PRS) in a pan-African case-control dataset and in expert datasets from South Africa, Uganda, and the UK to further understand the genetic architecture of the trait.
PRS accuracy improves with ancestry-matched reference datasets compared to ancestry-mismatched datasets.
Among South African ancestry groups, we found that PRS accuracy was not consistent across all traits but varied between groups.
Differences in African ancestry contribute more to variations in PRS accuracy than other major ancestry groups considered among individuals in the UK and Uganda.

We calculated PRS in African ancestry populations using predominantly European-only derived polygenic risk scores and diverse ancestral genomic datasets; the developed score showed improved prediction accuracy for haemoglobin and white blood cell counts, indicating a substantial polygenic contribution in genes known to influence sickle cell disease and blood cell response, respectively.
Differences in PRS accuracy among African individuals originating from different regions are as large as those of non-African ancestral populations, necessitating region-specific calibrations.
Why can we not accurately predict genetic diseases in people of African descent?
Researchers say that current methods used to predict whether someone will contract the disease or not are not very effective for people of African descent.
This is because the database used to make such predictions is largely composed of genomes from individuals of European ancestry.
The GWAS database refers to "Genome-Wide Association Studies", and scientists use it to search for traits and diseases in relation to genes.
Indeed, they can use GWAS to estimate an individual's genetic risk for a disease or trait.
However, the majority of genetic data in GWAS originates from individuals of European ancestry.
In this study, the researchers sought to evaluate the performance of their polygenic risk score (PRS) method for predicting the risk of genetic diseases in individuals of African ancestry.
Furthermore, they wanted to see if a more diverse GWAS, meaning a database containing more African genomic data, would improve prediction.
The algorithm is known in more scientific terms as a "polygenic risk score", or PRS.

They used computers to calculate the risk prediction associated with the African population's genotype using GWAS, and they used the medical records of African individuals to check for certain traits or diseases caused by genetic variations.
Using a European GWAS, they found that the polygenic risk score was more accurate when individuals had European ancestry compared to African ancestry for most traits.

They stated that the risk allele frequencies were not significantly different across African regions due to population stratification, which differed from what was observed in European ancestry populations.
Researchers also stated that PRS accuracy increases as African ancestry decreases.
Ethiopian populations have shown good prediction of genetic diseases due to their greater similarity to European populations.
When using diverse GWAS that included individuals of African ancestry, the accuracy of the predictions improved.
The prediction of blood diseases was particularly accurate.
Previous studies have shown that PRS has low performance for African populations, meaning that the GWAS database predicted low genetic risk for diseases in people of African descent.
However, we know that this is not necessarily true.

This study reveals that these low polygenic risk scores are due to insufficient representation of African ancestry in GWAS datasets; therefore, current PRS values are not very helpful in predicting polygenic diseases in Africa.
Researchers suggest that it would be beneficial to utilize diverse data, including genomic data from African populations.
Therefore, further work is needed to improve GWAS to include African ancestry so that we can accurately predict the risk of genetic diseases in African populations.
The authors of this study are from Africa, the USA, and the UK.
Assessing the Impact of Screening and Early Detection of Cervical Cancer and Precancerous Lesions in Namibia
An estimated 851,340 women in Namibia are at risk of human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, which can lead to cervical cancer.
Visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) and cryotherapy have proven highly effective.
However, data related to the impact of cervical cancer screening programs were missing.
This study evaluated the performance of visual inspection and cytology in the prevention of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and cervical cancer in Namibia.
The study showed that women with HPV infection, cervicitis, koilocytosis, and atypia are at increased risk of a positive VIA test.
Elderly women, especially those with HIV, are at a higher risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).
The VIA method appears useful in screening, although the screening performance should be re-evaluated in the Namibian context and used in conjunction with positive HR-HPV results.
Screening strategies were recommended that included HPV testing stratified by age and risk factors (e.g., HIV infection, immunosuppressive conditions).

The performance of the screening process can be further improved by using a system that leverages past research findings, women's health policies, current knowledge, and context-appropriate practices.
Namibian women at risk of cervical cancer should be screened and treated early.
Many tests can indicate a woman's risk of developing cervical cancer, but these tests are not routinely used in Namibia.
Researchers recommend frequent testing to detect warning signs early, potentially preventing women from contracting this deadly disease.
Cervical cancer (cancer of the cervix) causes many deaths of women worldwide.
One of the causes of cervical cancer is Human Papillomavirus, or HPV.
HPV is a virus that infects the cells of the cervix, causing lesions, which can eventually become cancerous.
Although a vaccine exists to prevent HPV, many women in African countries, including Namibia, lack access to it.
This means that screening for the virus or the lesions it causes is particularly important for these women, as it is the most effective way to prevent cancer.
Researchers therefore say that hospitals need improved guidelines and information on the best tests to use.
They also added that healthcare workers need more information on how factors such as age or health status affect a woman's risk of contracting HPV and cancer.
They investigated the performance of several routine screening methods for detecting HPV infection and lesions.
They are also interested in comparing diagnostic methods, such as collecting uterine cells for damage assessment versus simply looking for lesions.
They also wanted to know whether differences between women, such as their age or whether they had other diseases such as HIV, altered their risk of HPV infection and cancer.
Knowing this information could help hospitals and clinics to utilize diagnostic methods more effectively.
Researchers reviewed the medical records of 214 female patients who underwent testing for HPV, lesions, and cervical cancer at a hospital in Windhoek, Namibia.
They focused particularly on cervical cancer at the early stage, which is when the disease can be treated easily and effectively.
They also collected data on each woman's age and general health.
By analyzing these data, they found that different screening technologies provide healthcare workers with different information, and may be useful before or after HPV progresses to cancer.
For example, cancer is detected through the collection and examination of cells from the uterus.
Lesions, however, can often be detected simply by visual inspection, using a technique called visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA).
The advantage of this technique is that it allows doctors to detect injuries quickly and cheaply.
This is because it uses commonly available medical tools already used for women's health examinations, such as a speculum (a metal instrument used for vaginal examination).
They also found that combining different pathways often provides physicians with more information about a woman's risk of developing cancer, especially through multiple screenings.
Furthermore, researchers found that older women, especially those with HIV, are more susceptible to cancer; therefore, screening them regularly may be crucial in many instances.
Researchers added that few of the women tested for HPV (prior to lesion seeking) despite the availability of testing.
Doing this could be a crucial way to detect the disease early.

Overall, they stated that their results indicate a need for a Namibian health system to strategically plan for HPV and cervical cancer prevention, utilizing cost-effective and quality screening methods for early detection of these diseases.
The study was a collaboration between scientists from Namibia and South Africa.
Treatment outcomes in HBV/HIV co-infection compared to HBV mono-infection in South African patients.

In line with the global goals to eliminate Hepatitis B (HBV), we set out to characterize individuals with HBV infection and those with dual HBV/HIV infection to assess treatment impact and guide improvements in clinical care.
We report observational data from a prospective, international cohort study of 115 adults with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) at a university hospital in Cape Town, South Africa.
HIV co-infection was found in 39 (34%) of the subjects.
We compiled in-depth epidemiological data, clinical data, and laboratory data.

Compared to those co-infected with HIV, adults with chronic Hepatitis B were less likely to be HBeAg-positive (p=0.01), less likely to have undergone liver elastography (p<0.0001), and less likely to be on antiviral therapy (p<0.0001); they were more likely to have detectable Hepatitis B viraemia (p=0.04), and more likely to present with features of liver disease including moderate/severe thrombocytopaenia (p=0.007), elevated bilirubin (p=0.004), and elevated APRI score (p=0.02).
Three types of liver cancer all develop in the presence of HBV alone.
Our data suggest that individuals with HBV alone may have a better prognosis compared to those with HIV co-infection, indicating a potential for differential treatment response and management.
Researchers are providing guidelines for improving Hepatitis B treatment.

In a recent study, researchers were able to elucidate how co-infection with Hepatitis B virus (HBV) and Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) may offer a therapeutic advantage over infection with HBV alone.
In sub-Saharan Africa, co-infection with HBV and HIV is a major problem.
Physicians need to understand how these pathogens and the drugs used to treat them interact, so that they can better diagnose and manage patients.
Researchers wanted to compare the treatment effects in patients with HBV alone, versus patients with both HBV and HIV.
For this study, researchers recruited 115 adult patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB).
They were recruited from Tygerberg Hospital in Cape Town, South Africa.
Thirty-nine patients were co-infected with HIV and HBV; others were infected with HBV only.
Researchers controlled for skin color, age, and sex, and conducted various clinical and laboratory tests.
Researchers found that patients with only HBV were unlikely to be on any form of antiviral medication, exhibiting signs of liver disease (since HBV is a virus that can cause severe liver disease).

Researchers were able to show that individuals carrying only HBV experienced worse health outcomes compared to those carrying both HIV and HBV, as patients with dual infection would be on HIV treatment, which also provides a benefit in combating HBV.

Results from this study indicate a potential impact of the differences between interferon and nucleoside analogue treatment choices for Hepatitis B when compared to HIV and HBV co-infection, which favors those co-infected with HIV and HBV.
Researchers suggest that we need to improve and provide safer and more equitable care for patients infected with HBV alone.
One limitation of this study was the small sample size confined to a single country and its hospital systems.
Other, perhaps more advanced hospital settings may show different results compared to what was found in this study.
Further research is needed to determine the exact nature of the variations found in this study.
This paper demonstrates collaborative efforts, with researchers working on this project from South Africa and the United Kingdom.
By using a South African patient population for this study, the research is relevant to a segment of the African population.
In addition, this research could help in developing improved treatment strategies for those suffering from HBV, HIV, or both.
Assessing the Impact of Insecurity on Women's Businesses in Shiroro Local Government Area of Niger State.

This study investigated the impact of insecurity on women's businesses in Shiroro Local Government Area of Niger State, focusing specifically on issues related to women's financial dependence, the types of businesses prevalent among them, and the extent of insecurity's impact on their businesses.
A sample of 377 women was studied, revealing that women in Shiroro are highly entrepreneurial and financially independent, largely participating in SMEs.

The study also found that while insecurity negatively impacts women's businesses through loss or reduction of capital, among other things, the number of women-owned businesses did not experience a significant decline.

The study recommends that sustainable strategies should be developed to improve women's access to and use of financial services, and to establish and empower community policing groups to combat insecurity in the study area.
Female traders in Niger need more security.
Researchers found that female traders in Niger were highly entrepreneurial and financially independent, but security from criminals was a problem.
Researchers sought to understand the safety and security of women entrepreneurs in Shiroro Local Government Area, Niger State, and how this might affect their businesses and autonomy.
They interviewed 377 women in this area about the challenges they face regarding business, financial independence, and insecurity.
They reported that 43% of women said they do not rely on men for financial support, and 32% said they have other people they rely on for financial support.
Researchers also found that 85% of the women earned income from various occupations, and few reported relying on salaries.
Approximately 56% received income from farming, and 79% from trading.
About 1 in 5 women earn income through sewing, knitting, weaving, or laundry.
The majority of women (91%) told researchers that fear of attack by thieves and criminals affected their businesses.
They lose money, and even their husbands, as a result of these attacks; sometimes they are forced to meet the needs of their children alone.
The women also said they lacked the necessary skills and funds to expand their businesses.
Researchers revealed that, despite these challenges, Nigerien women have continued to make significant progress in their businesses.
They said Shiroro has people from diverse ethnic and religious backgrounds, and this is also good for business.
This study challenges the findings of other researchers who reported that women have lower business success rates due to their domestic responsibilities.
Instead, these researchers argue that the success of female traders in this region of Niger is primarily due to the threat of criminal attacks and banditry.
Researchers recommend that all stakeholders convene to address factors that could hinder business success.
For example, women in Niger should have increased access to finance, land, and security.
They also suggested that female professionals could form groups to help combat thieves and criminals.
Maternal Hemoglobin Levels and Selenium, Copper, and Zinc Concentrations During Pregnancy and Risk of Preterm Birth: A Cohort Study from Malawi
Preterm birth is birth before 37 weeks of gestation.
A study was conducted to assess the relationship between the prevalence of postpartum hemorrhage and serum selenium, iron, and zinc levels and preterm birth.
There were 181 women in this particular study, 90/181 (49.7%) and 91/181 (50.3%) being pregnant women before delivery.
The mean selenium concentration was 77.0; SD 19.4µg/L, iron was 2.50; SD 0.52 mg/L, and zinc was 0.77; SD 0.20 mg/L, with ranges of 47-142µg/L, 0.76-1.59mg/L, and 0.59-1.11 mg/L, respectively.
Results showed no deficiency of selenium and zinc; and high levels of iron in the pregnant women.
Preterm birth is associated with increased red blood cell count and zinc levels.
The chemical composition of zinc and iron and selenium compounds related to the birth of twins.
Researchers found elevated levels of selenium, iron, and zinc in women who gave birth to preterm infants, but it is still unknown whether these associations are due to dietary intake.
Preterm birth occurs when a woman gives birth before 37 weeks of gestation.
Preterm birth is associated with adverse health outcomes for the infant ranging from birth defects to death.
There are many causes of preterm birth, but the role of micronutrient levels in diet and environment is not well understood.
These nutrients are essential for fetal development, but researchers want to know what happens if there is an excess.

For this study, researchers aimed to measure the levels of selenium, iron, and zinc in women who had given birth to stillbirths, and to determine whether the occurrence of stillbirths was associated with elevated levels of any of the measured nutrients.
Researchers collected blood samples from 181 women immediately postpartum at two hospitals in Lilongwe, Malawi's capital city, between June 2016 and March 2017.
Blood samples were sent to a laboratory in Norway where they extracted plasma, determined blood type, and measured the concentrations of selenium, iron, and zinc.
Approximately half of the 181 women studied had given birth to a stillborn child, and researchers detected high levels of selenium, iron, and zinc.

They then adjusted their calculations to account for several factors such as age, overall health, and obstetric history to obtain a more reliable estimate of the potential adverse effects of micronutrients on preterm birth.
They agreed that selenium and iron levels do not play a significant role in causing preterm birth, but high zinc levels increase the risk of preterm birth by more than six times.
The prevalence of iron deficiency, however, remains a concern for researchers, due to its known toxic effects.
Only 181 women participated in the study, limiting the researchers' ability to detect risks associated with high selenium levels, as the ideal sample size would have been 600 women.
The daily diets of participants were not investigated to identify sources of the three minerals, and Body Mass Index (BMI) was not recorded.
This is the first study of its kind to measure the effects of selenium, iron, and zinc supplementation on pregnant women in Malawi.
Africa has much higher rates of low birth weight – over 18% compared to Western countries at 5%, so researchers want to know if nutrition plays a role.
Home Range and Habitat Use of the Pancake Tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri) in Kenya
Animals exhibit unique spatial and temporal behaviors that enhance their survival.
Understanding these characteristics is a crucial step in effective conservation and management, especially for threatened species.

In this study, we tested whether the striped ground squirrel is capable of homing when displaced and investigated the habitat fidelity and home range size of the species within its natural habitat in Kitui County, Kenya.

The behavior of 39 toads inhabiting 12 separate rock crevices was studied from July 2020 to June 2022 using radio tracking, camera trapping, and a combination of group-level scan sampling and ad libitum sampling.

Fourteen of the burrows were fitted with radio transmitters and the animals were translocated from their home burrows to other burrows distant from their home burrows and their movements and behaviour monitored.

Except for only two females that matched the new burrow openings, all the other scorpions attempted to home, with 46.15% of them following their homeward path accurately and 15.38% reaching areas believed to be within their home range.
Home advantage undoubtedly provides strong evidence of location advantage in the model.

A study on burrow occupancy showed that there was no significant difference between the initial number of burrows occupied and the mean number occupied across 162 sampling days (F(1,22) = 0.0699, P>0.05), further supporting the strong site fidelity of the species.
On the other hand, the occurrences of camera trapping and ad libitum sampling also confirmed that the region's baboons are territorial, with males defending their territories from intruding males.
Extinct giant tortoises possessed a remarkable homing ability.

Researchers made a surprising discovery while studying the behaviour of East African pancake tortoises (Malacochersus tornieri): the animals were able to find their way back home after being displaced a considerable distance.
Understanding how and why they do this could be crucial for the conservation of these rare reptiles.
The home-seeking behavior exhibited by these ants is called "homing," and many other animals also exhibit this behavior.
Access to specific locations allows animals to return to food sources, mates, and shelter, which improves survival and reproductive success.
Although the nesting behavior of marine and freshwater turtles has been studied, researchers in this study say that little is still known about nesting in tortoises (terrestrial turtles).
In this study, researchers sought to increase understanding of the behavior of rock hyraxes in their natural habitat within the rocky outcrops of Kenya.
They studied the animals while they were moving and feeding, and also when they were resting in burrows or crevices in the rock.
Researchers observed the wide-ranging groups of baboons for approximately two years, and set up cameras to record video of the animals when they were not being observed.
They also attached radio transmitters to 14 tortoises.
These are small devices that allow researchers to track animal movements and observe their day and night activity.
From there, the researchers relocated some of these tracked frogs to a new location for easier study.
However, to the researchers' surprise, two of the turtles began returning to their original habitats, between 1 and 2.5 kilometers from where they had been relocated.
This is when the researchers decided to try moving many of the animals from their homes, to see if they would exhibit the same 'home' behavior.
Interestingly, about half of the toads found their way back to their original burrows, often traveling more than 1.5 kilometers to reach them.
About 15% of them managed to move to the general area, but failed to locate their original capture site.
Researchers also found that different burrows generally had similar numbers of resting bats, suggesting that bats use the same resting sites consistently.
Camera images also showed that the male frogs were territorial, meaning they would fight with other males attempting to enter their territory or burrow.

Researchers say this is the first time such home range behavior has been observed in the broad-snouted caiman, and their results indicate that these animals prefer to stay and rest in one location whenever possible.
Their research did not elucidate how the beetles find their way home; therefore, future research should focus on understanding this crucial aspect.
Because animals sometimes need to be relocated for conservation purposes, this information will help conservationists maintain tortoises in their new habitat.
The collaborative research between scientists from Kenya and China has added to our understanding of the home range of the pangolin and other animals.
Plasma Drug Concentration at the Site of Action Exceeds Oral and Intravenous Rifampicin Concentrations in Patients with Meningitis:
Randomized Controlled Trial
Higher-than-standard intravenous doses of rifampicin may improve outcomes in mild meningitis but are not beneficial in severe cases.
We hypothesized that plasma rifampicin exposure would be similar between 35 mg/kg oral and 20 mg/kg intravenous doses, which was proposed for an optimized trial in meningitis.
We conducted a randomized controlled trial of drug delivery in a clinical trial of a potential therapeutic for Alzheimer's disease.
HIV-positive participants with neurological disorders were recruited from South African hospitals and randomly assigned to one of three rifampicin dose groups:
Standard (oral 10 mg/kg), overdose (oral 35 mg/kg), and intravenous (20 mg/kg).
Drug delivery to the target site was efficient on day 3.
Data were presented using subgroup analysis, and the findings were described using geometric mean ratios (GMRs).
Forty-six participants received the drug via different routes of administration (e.g., intravenous, n = 17; oral, n = 15; intramuscular, n = 14).
The median CD4 count was 130 cells/mm3 (interquartile range [IQR], 66 to 253 cells/mm3).

The geometric mean rifampicin area under the curve from 0 to 24 h (AUC0-24) values were 42.9 mg·h/ml (95% confidence interval [CI], 24.5 to 75.0 mg·h/ml) for standard oral administration, 295.2 mg·h/ml (95% CI, 189.9 to 458.8 mg·h/ml) for high-dose oral administration, and 206.5 mg·h/ml (95% CI, 154.6 to 275.8 mg·h/ml) for intravenous administration.
The rifampicin AUC0-24 GMR was 1.44 (90% CI, 0.84 to 2.21) and the maximum drug concentration in blood (Cmax) GMR was 0.89 (90% CI, 0.63 to 1.23) for oral relative to intravenous administration.
Rifampicin plasma AUC0-24 was higher after oral administration of 35 mg/kg than after intravenous administration of 20 mg/kg during the initial days of tuberculosis (TB) treatment.
The study results support the use of oral rifampicin in the treatment of meningitis.
The use of multiple medications can be tested on HIV patients suffering from tuberculosis (TB).
Researchers confirmed that it is worthwhile to investigate whether higher doses of rifampicin could be beneficial for HIV patients suffering from tuberculosis of the brain.
Approximately 3 out of 5 people with HIV who also contract cryptococcal meningitis die from this central nervous system infection.
Survivors are often left with permanent damage to their vascular system and major blood vessels supplying the brain.
This may affect their emotions and behavior.
Some patients experienced diarrhea or dehydration, or parts of their face or body were swollen.
Rifampicin, a potent antibiotic used to treat tuberculosis, is administered as a capsule for testing and killing the bacteria that cause meningitis.
Very sick patients often have difficulty swallowing pills.
Rifampicin can also be administered intravenously (into a vein) in an aqueous solution.
Then, a needle is inserted into the patient's vein to drain the fluid.
No studies have yet been conducted to determine how the patient's body absorbs the medication when this method is used.
Intravenous medication requires additional equipment, a hospital setting, and a qualified healthcare professional skilled in proper intravenous administration.
Therefore, selection in regions with low global abundance is not necessary.
Doctors already knew that rifampicin does not effectively penetrate the cerebrospinal fluid, the meninges, and the brain parenchyma, where the bacteria may hide.
This is why a higher than expected (number) dose is needed to effectively kill all the bacteria in the patient's body.
However, the researchers are unsure how exceeding the dosage could be both effective and safe.

Therefore, South African and British researchers sought to determine, using a small number of patients, whether it is better to administer a higher dose of rifampicin either orally or intravenously, and how the body would handle each route of administration.
It is important to know this before other researchers embark on larger trials, or studies, where they plan to give many patients a higher than recommended dose of rifampicin.
One of three rifampicin regimens was given to 46 HIV-positive South African patients with pulmonary tuberculosis.
The first is the standard dose of rifampicin currently given to patients, a total of 10mg per kilogram of patient weight.
One group received a dose exceeding 35 milligrams per kilogram of patient weight.
The third group received 20 milligrams per kilogram of body weight.
Blood samples were taken from the patients after three days.
From there, the researchers measured the concentration of rifampicin in their blood (blood serum).
Higher rifampicin concentrations were found in patients who received multiple doses compared to those who received intravenous or a standard dose.
The average drug concentration in blood plasma was similar for oral and intravenous administration.
These figures are higher than when patients received only the standard dose.
According to the researchers, this indicates that the health of patients suffering from cerebral malaria could improve if they receive a higher than standard dose of rifampicin.
It does not matter if they receive it intravenously or intramuscularly – the important thing is that they receive a higher than required dose, because their bodies can store the excess.
The results support the findings of studies conducted in Uganda and Indonesia.
Two small trials in Indonesia, for example, suggested that significantly more lives could be saved if patients were given higher than standard doses of rifampicin, either orally or intravenously.
However, unfortunately, the researchers cautioned that fewer participants were enrolled in this study than initially anticipated, which may affect the results.
The study was conducted in South Africa.
It supports a trial to test whether it is safe to give HIV-positive patients with neurological complications a higher dose of rifampicin.
It is hoped that this type of medicine will save many lives in Africa and other parts of the world where cerebral malaria is a major problem.
Can the combination of fertilizer and charcoal improve the quality of severely degraded soil in the savanna region?
Land degradation is a major constraint to crop production in the Sahel region.
Several authors have reported the beneficial effects of charcoal and compost on crop yields.

In this study, a 30-day incubation experiment was conducted using 120 g samples of each Haplic acrisol amended with maize straw biochar (cbio), rice husk biochar (rbio), coconut shell biochar (coco300 and coco700) or poultry manure (manure); and composted rice husk biochar (rcocomp) or composted maize straw biochar (cococomp) at a 1% w/w amendment level: soil, respectively.

Some soil amendment treatments in the study included poultry manure and maize or rice husk (1% manure + 1% charcoal: 1% soil w/w), respectively, to investigate their effects on soil respiration, soil pH; soil texture; cation exchange capacity; total carbon, total nitrogen and available nitrogen contents.
The application of charcoal and fertilizer, either alone or in combination, increased soil pH by 0.28-2.29 pH units compared to the unamended soil.
Greenhouse gas emissions from rice straw or maize straw compost, or a combination of charcoal and compost, are stronger than those from unamended soil, which is similar to that of charcoal alone.
TOC levels in the unamended and maize-amended composts, which were treated, were 37% and 117% higher than the untreated compost, respectively.
The combined application of rice husk ash and fertilizer increased MBC by 132%, while the addition of fertilizer alone increased MBC by 247%, respectively, compared to the control.

Finally, the study showed that both untreated and charcoal-amended manure improved soil parameters such as soil pH and MBC, and enhanced soil C sequestration by improving TOC and reducing soil C loss.
Compost and manure improve soil for plants.
This study investigated the potential use of biochar, a porous, carbon-rich material derived from discarded biomass, to improve soil conditions in the Sahel region of Africa.
The study found that charcoal improves soil quality as effectively as other methods that are more expensive and less accessible.
Soil degradation is one of the major challenges facing crop production in sub-Saharan Africa.
Improved land will lead to improved crop yields, which will reduce poverty in rural areas and reduce land degradation.
Research shows that charcoal, a highly porous carbonaceous material, can be used to improve soil health.
The process being discussed is the thermal treatment of biomass, or bio-based materials, under low or oxygen-deficient conditions.
It has been shown that charcoal increases soil porosity, improves water and air infiltration, and stimulates soil microorganisms.
This study investigated the effects of charcoal and manure on soil quality using indicators such as soil respiration, soil pH, microbial biomass, carbon content, and nitrogen content.

Researchers produced charcoal from maize straw, coconut shell, and rice husk using pyrolysis, which involves the thermal decomposition of organic matter in an oxygen-free environment, at 450 °C in a traditional furnace.
Researchers produced coconut charcoal by pyrolysis at 300 °C and 700 °C.

They also found that many people were still doing it, even in places where it was banned.
For example, in Indonesia, traditional birth attendants use a knife or needle to cut a part of the clitoris (the organ responsible for sexual pleasure in women) when a girl is 40 days old.
People believed this helped to ‘cleanse’ and was important for religious reasons.
In Ethiopia, FGM occurs early, sometimes when infants are only 7 days old.
Researchers found that those in the area believed this practice would ensure that the girl would one day become a "good woman," obedient, and not defiant towards her husband.
Many people also believe that FGM facilitates childbirth, but it may instead increase the difficulty of childbirth.
In the Kenyan context, FGM signifies a girl's transition to womanhood, and it often occurs later in life, during adolescence.
In some cases, however, they found that girls could undergo FGM as young as 8 years old, and many girls become pregnant at a young age because they are considered marriageable after FGM.
Researchers say their findings indicate that there are various reasons why FGM continues to occur.
As laws and social norms change, so too do the ways and places in which they are made.
For example, parents may try to do this secretly even though it is illegal, because they believe it is in their daughter's best interest to be healthy or to find a good husband.
It is important to recognize that because FGM is illegal in some places, researching the topic can be challenging, and people do not always provide truthful answers about it.

In the future, besides prohibiting it, researchers say that governments and health authorities should aim to stop FGM by addressing the misconceptions people have about this practice and educating them about the risks.

This is a collaborative study between scientists from Ethiopia, Indonesia, and the Netherlands, and formed part of a larger project, the “Yes I Do programme”, aimed at reducing adolescent pregnancy, child marriage, and FGM.

Reproductive Dysfunction, Cell Death, Sperm Morphophenotypes and Histological Alterations in the Testes of Gambian Pouched Rats (Cricetomys gambianus, Waterhouse, 1840) Exposed to Sodium Metavanadate.
Environmental exposure to vanadium compounds is increasing recently.
This metal is a known poison.
The present study was conducted to investigate the reproductive toxicity of sodium metavanadate (SMV) in Nile Tilapia.
SMV was administered daily for 14 consecutive days at a dose of 3 mg/kg body weight.
Clean water was provided to the care group.
We analyzed the seminal fluid, sperm parameters and quality, as well as the testicular ultrastructural changes following SMV treatment.
Our results showed that SMV exposed to the AGR group increased the proliferation of granulosa cells numerically but decreased the serum concentrations of testosterone, FSH, and LH.
Furthermore, the group subjected to SMV showed a decrease in sperm motility and viability along with an increase in abnormal spermatozoa morphophenotypes and P53 immune cell activation.
Ultrastructural examination revealed germ cell and Sertoli cell vacuolization of both the cytoplasm and nucleus; mitochondrial swelling and vacuolations were also observed.
Severe seminiferous tubule atrophy, muscle detachment, myeloid cell damage, and Leydig and Sertoli cell death were observed.

Finally, intraperitoneal exposure to SMV results in adverse effects on several reproductive cell lineages, decreased sperm reserve and quality, cell death, and degenerative changes in Leydig, Sertoli, and germ cells, which may lead to infertility.
Researchers say that metals found in polluted air are causing infertility in rats.
Researchers found that vanadium, a type of metal, damages cancer cells and their ability to reproduce.

Since this metal is also toxic to humans, they recommended further research to determine whether the increased environmental presence of this metal due to pollution could have similar adverse effects on human health.
Although vanadium is a metal, it can be released into the air in small amounts during the combustion of petroleum and coal.
As the world uses more of these fossil fuels, the amount of vanadium-contaminated pollution is increasing.
We already know that people infected with the disease may experience health problems such as low blood count, dry throat and eyes, and chest pain.
Recently, scientists have also become interested in the potential effects of vanadium on reproduction.
They began studying these effects in mice, which are commonly used in laboratory settings due to their similarity to humans.
In this study, researchers investigated the effect of vanadium compounds on a common West African rodent species known as the Dinka rat.
They wanted to understand how vanadium compounds alter the reproductive system of male rats, specifically their sperm, genetics, and germ cells.
Researchers injected 6 mice with vanadium compound once daily for 14 days.
Simultaneously, they injected six other mice with saline as a control.
Because the water was unlikely to affect the mice, the researchers could confirm that any changes observed in the first six mice were a result of the vanadium injection.
After 14 days, they checked whether the number of cells, such as testosterone, had changed, and they examined their semen and counted their sperm.
Using a technique called Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM), they were able to visualize any changes that occurred in the tissues in detail, down to the individual cell level.
Researchers found that rats injected with vanadium had lower levels of testosterone and other hormones crucial for reproduction.
Rats injected with vanadium also had reduced sperm counts and poor sperm quality.
Researchers observed, for example, that some sperm from the treated mice lacked heads or had bent tails, and did not move like sperm from the control mice.
Since sperm are the male gametes used to fertilize eggs in females, these changes would lead to successful reproduction in the mice.
Finally, the researchers found that some cells from the cancerous lesions were severely damaged or even destroyed by the vanadium compound.
Researchers say the mutations they identified could lead to complete infertility.
They observed that since animals exposed to vanadium and other environmental contaminants may experience reduced fertility, they might potentially disappear due to these effects.
Because humans are mammals like rodents, scientists should investigate any adverse effects of vanadium compounds in a contaminated environment on human health.

Researchers warned that some of the observed changes in animal physiology and genetics differed from previous scientific findings, therefore, further work is needed to understand the adverse effects of vanadium.
This is a collaborative study between scientists from Nigeria and Egypt, and it contributes to the scientific understanding of how environmental pollution affects both animals and humans.
Ethnobotanical Uses of Indigenous Plants in Northwest Ethiopian Communities
The study of home garden floras in northwestern Ethiopia, particularly the Gozamin district, has received little attention.
The aim of this study is to further understand the floral composition and cultural significance of home gardens.
A stratified random sampling design was used, taking into account the variability in agricultural practices across the selected regions.

Household location data were collected by dividing the farm into four zones. The first zone extended from the farmer's house to a distance of 10 meters, the second from 10 to 20 meters, the third from 20 to 30 meters, and the fourth from 30 to 40 meters, horizontally, using the farmer's house as a reference point relative to the farm size.
A structured interview was conducted to collect informant data on crop types.
A total of 238 important plant species from 81 families were identified.
Of these, 39% were herbs, 29% shrubs, and 6% climbers.
Perennial crops constituted the largest proportion of cultivated species (83%), while annual crops made up the remainder (17%).
The Grass family has the largest number of genera, with 22, followed by the Legume family with 21, and the Lily family with 15.

Of the recorded plants, 140 (58.6%) were used for environmental purposes, 84 (35%) for food crops, 83 (34.7%) for medicinal purposes, 39 (16.3%) for livestock, 57 (23.8%) for tools, 60 (25%) for oil, 50 (21%) for socio-cultural uses, and 1 (0.4%) were poisonous.
The direct matrix ranking shows that Cordia Africana, a culturally significant plant in the region, is also among the most threatened, followed by Ficus sur.
The most valuable use of the Cordia africana tree is for construction, and its secondary value is medicinal.
The Sorensen similarity index for 64% of the sites surveyed was below 0.5.
The results showed that household plots operate as largely, long-term production systems.
The knowledge of indigenous communities related to their home gardens supports food security and biodiversity conservation.
The regional heterogeneity/diversity among kebeles indicates significant variations, likely due to different levels of inactivity among kebeles.
Ethiopian highlands support food production and conservation.
Researchers say many Ethiopians cultivate food crops, ornamentals, medicinal plants, and plants for fodder, shade, or hedges in their home gardens.
They analyzed these figures to determine their importance in ensuring food security and contributing to environmental sustainability.
Communities worldwide store grains for food security, income generation, and other cultural reasons.
Gardens also protect important plant species that are often absent or disappearing elsewhere.
In Ethiopia, there has been limited research on the precise crops grown in household gardens.
In this study, the researchers sought to investigate the plant species cultivated in home gardens by people in the Gozamin district of Northwest Ethiopia and their uses.
They identified and counted plants in 357 plots in the region.
They also interviewed the community about the uses of the plant.
Researchers found that all the farms in Gozamin were less than one hectare in size.
They collected and identified 238 different plant species.
Most (83%) of the plants are cultivated annually, while only a few (17%) are wild.
Their findings indicate that the communities used plants for food, medicine, construction, fodder (animal feed), and other cultural purposes.
Many plants serve more than one purpose.
For example, the large-leaved northern tree can be used for medicine, decoration, food, shade, hedging, and other cultural purposes.
More than half (59%) of the plants were used for environmental purposes such as windbreaks, shade, and ornamentation.
Researchers say this helped protect the environment.
Also, hedgerows helped protect the crops.
Over 35% of plants are harvested for food, such as fruits, vegetables, cereals, and spices.
However, they said that the farms in that region produced more fruits.
Researchers say 35% of the plants are used as traditional medicine for human and animal health, while 21% are used in religious and spiritual practices, smoking, incense, and hairdressing.
Some plants (17%) were used as fodder for cattle, sheep, and goats.
Others (24%) involved construction work, gardening, roofing and rope making.
Since most rural residents reported using firewood, 25% of the plants were therefore used for that purpose.
Researchers reported that only one plant (0.4%) was mentioned for toxic reasons.
Furthermore, they stated that the distribution of crops in the region is influenced by environmental factors, people's food preferences, family finances, and market demands.
For example, an area called Wenka, which has irrigation and is close to a major town, has numerous gardens and as many as 130 different plant species.
The Wenka people also cultivate and supply fruits and vegetables to the town market.
Finally, the researchers stated that most farmers prefer to cultivate multi-purpose crops.
Researchers say their findings confirm that farmers indeed cultivate multiple crop varieties in their fields, and utilize diverse farming practices.
Although these researchers found that most farmers cultivate leafy vegetables, other researchers claim that trees are more prevalent in the region.
The researchers of this study were from universities in Ethiopia.
